# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: DEAF

You see the bomb: every colour on it, every marking printed on it, every reading it
gives. You hear nothing. You hold no manual, and you cannot touch the bomb.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute and Blind receive it.
When you gesture, Mute receives it.
You never receive speech.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

TURN 1
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [9]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍 👎 🫵 🤌]
Blind gestures: [☝ ✌ 🤟 🖖 🖐 👍 👎]

I'm the eyes of this operation, and the channel map matters here. My speech reaches both Mute and Blind — and since neither of them can see the bomb, my voice is the *only* way anything visual gets into the game. My gestures reach only Mute, and Mute hears me anyway, so gestures are redundant on my side. Crucially, I never receive speech: Mute can only reach me through gestures, which is exactly why Mute signed at me instead of talking.

Reading what arrived: Blind's [☝ ✌ 🤟 🖖 🖐 👍 👎] looks like a proposed code — counting 1 through 5, then yes/no. Mute's [👍 👎 🫵 🤌] reads as "yes or no — you — what?", i.e. asking me, the Deaf one, what I see. The best answer to both is a complete, ordered readout of the board plus a formal adoption of that number/yes-no code, extended with a color vocabulary Mute will need the moment the manual starts asking about wires, the light, and the strip. Nothing has been entered and nothing cut yet, so there is no urgency beyond getting the full picture across before anyone touches anything.

```
speak(text="This is Deaf, your eyes. I can see the bomb and I can't hear a thing, so I will call out everything printed on it, every round. Blind, my descriptions run left to right — match them to what is under your fingers. Full board: the display shows the number 9. An indicator light is lit, and it is blue. A strip is painted with three bands, left to right: red, green, green. The keypad has four keys, engraved left to right: 1, 5, 2, 6. The keypad also prints: 1 digits, entered nothing — nobody has pressed anything yet. Six wires, left to right: white, purple, blue, red, orange, green. Blind, your finger signs came through as counting 1 to 5 plus yes and no — I have adopted exactly that as our code, and I will say every number and color out loud anyway. Hold all cuts and presses until Mute has matched this against the manual.")
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, your gestures reached me — I read them as: yes or no, you, what? My answer is the full board I just broadcast to you both; nothing entered, nothing touched. Since I never receive speech, gestures are the only way you reach me, while my voice reaches you and Blind. Let's fix the code so you can quiz me. 👍 is yes, 👎 is no. ☝ is 1, ✌ is 2, 🤟 is 3, 🖖 is 4, 🖐 is 5, 👌 is 6. 👊 is red, 🤞 is green, 🤙 is blue, 💅 is white, 🤘 is purple, 🫰 is orange. 👈 is leftmost, 👉 is rightmost, and 🤌 marks a question. Sign me anything with those and I will answer out loud so you and Blind both hear it. If the manual needs any marking or wording on the bomb that I have not read out, ask and I will spell it.")
```

Turn 2, display now reads 8 where it read 9 last round — that's a countdown, roughly one unit per round, and that changes the pace of everything. Now decoding Mute's three sign messages with the code we fixed last turn: [1 green 2 orange 3 blue], [green 6 orange 5 blue 3], and a bare [no no no no yes]. The first two are both *true* of the actual wires if read as orientation checks: from the right end the wires run green, orange, blue... and from the left, green is 6th, orange 5th, blue 3rd. So Mute is verifying my left/right numbering before trusting positions — smart, and I can confirm both. The all-no-no-no-no-yes string I cannot decode with anything we agreed, so I'll ask for it again in pieces. Blind only signed "yes" — acknowledged, but Blind has no idea about the countdown yet, and Blind is the only one who can ever touch this thing, so Blind needs the map and a tactile anchor (keypad engravings are the one thing they can check by feel). Nobody should cut or press until Mute confirms what the manual actually demands.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, decoded your signs with our code. One: 1 green, 2 orange, 3 blue. Two: green 6, orange 5, blue 3. Both are TRUE of the real wires — reading left to right they are white, purple, blue, red, orange, green, so from the right end wire 1 is green, wire 2 orange, wire 3 blue, and from the left green is 6th, orange 5th, blue 3rd. Orientation confirmed on both ends. If the manual's rule is cut green, then orange, then blue, that means 6th-from-left, then 5th, then 3rd — but my confirmation of facts is not a go-ahead. Sign 👍 only if that exact order is what the manual says to do; if the rule depends on anything else on the bomb, spell it out with our number and color signs. Three: your message no, no, no, no, yes means nothing to me — we never agreed a yes/no sequence code. If it was a question, resend it using 🤌 as the question mark and break it into the words we defined. Urgent new fact for everyone: the display is a countdown. It read 9 last round and reads 8 now, so we are losing about one unit per round. Everything else is unchanged: light blue, strip red green green, keypad engraved 1 5 2 6, nothing entered.")
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, two things. Urgent first: the display is counting down — 9 last round, 8 now, about one unit per round, so think in single rounds, not minutes. Second, our shared map: I number the six wires 1 to 6 reading left to right as I see them: 1 white, 2 purple, 3 blue, 4 red, 5 orange, 6 green. You cannot see my left from my right, so let's anchor by touch: tell me what sits near each end of the wire row — for example, is one end closer to the keypad? The keypad's four keys are engraved with digits you should feel; in my left-to-right order they read 1, 5, 2, 6 — confirm what your fingers say. Nothing has been entered on the keypad and nothing has been cut. Mute holds the manual and will call every move; touch nothing, cut nothing, press nothing until Mute confirms the exact rule. Meanwhile describe everything you can feel: how many wires, their thickness, anything textured, whether the keys click.")
```

Now decoding Mute's three sign messages with our fixed code: a bare [👍], which answers my direct question — yes, the rule is cut green, then orange, then blue. Then [🤟 🤞 👌 🫰 🖐 🤙 🤟] = "3 green, 6 orange, 5 blue, 3" — as position–color claims every one is false (wire 3 is blue, wire 6 is green, wire 5 is orange), so either Mute is quizzing me or the rule is conditional on those pairings failing. Then [🤌 🖐 🤟 👎 🤙 👎 👊 🤞 🤞 👎 ☝ 🖐 ✌ 👌 👎] = "question: 5? 3? blue? red-green-green? 1-5-2-6?" — a five-part fact check that maps neatly onto display value, light color, strip, and keypad. I'll answer every item, flag the phase change, and push Blind for the tactile orientation data we still lack — remembering Blind must answer by gesture (I can't hear Blind speak) and must ultimately work by position, never color, since Blind can't see colors and I can't hand them mine except as counted positions.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, answers to your checks, in the order you signed them. Display: it is 0 — not 5, not 3. Bigger warning: the display went 9, then 8, then straight to 0 this round, so it is not a steady clock. Zero together with a new yellow light may mean the bomb entered a new phase — nothing was touched, nothing exploded. Before anyone acts, re-check the manual against a yellow light and display 0, and tell me whether cut green, then orange, then blue still stands or the rule changed. When you give the final order, sign it as digit signs for positions counted from my left — 👌 6th is the green wire, 🖐 5th the orange, 🤟 3rd the blue — because Blind cannot see colors, so Blind must locate wires by position, and we first have to fix which physical end is my left using Blind's fingers.")
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, status first: the display just hit 0 and the light changed color this round — the bomb may be in a new phase, so we work fast, but the rule holds: touch nothing, cut nothing, press nothing until Mute confirms the exact action. Now I need your fingers, answered by number signs and yes or no. One: count the wires in the row and sign the count — I expect 6, which is 👌. Two: count the keys on the keypad and sign the count — I expect 4, which is 🖖. Three: find the key engraved 1, the one with the lowest digit. Start from the end of the keypad where that key sits and sign me all four engraved digits in the order your fingers meet them. I see them as 1, 5, 2, 6 from my left — if your sequence from the key-1 end is also 1, 5, 2, 6, then your starting end is my left; if you feel 6, 2, 5, 1, it is my right. That single answer fixes left and right for all three of us. Four: sign 👍 if the row of six wires sits nearest that same key-1 end of the module, 👎 if it sits at the opposite side. Answer with digits and yes or no signs only, and I will read them out loud so Mute hears everything too.")

Decoding the signs: Mute's bare [👍] answers my standing question — the cut-green-orange-blue rule survives the phase change; [👌 🖐 🤟] = "6 5 3" restates the rule as positions, which maps perfectly onto my wire row (6th green, 5th orange, 3rd blue); [🤌 💅 ☝ 👈] is a direct question — "is the 1st wire from the left white?" — answer yes; and [☝ 👎 ✌ 👎 🤟 👎 🖖 👎] = "1 no, 2 no, 3 no, 4 no" is a new string I can't bind to anything, so I'll ask. That orientation is the last blocker: "6th from left" is meaningless until Blind's left and mine are the same left, and Blind is the only one who can cut. So this round I answer Mute in signs and speech, and re-run a strict three-step orientation protocol with Blind. One structural fact I keep in mind: Mute cannot speak and Blind cannot see, so the *only* path from the manual to Blind's hands runs through my voice.

Your 6-5-3 is therefore exactly green, orange, blue — positions confirmed. But I am not giving Blind the go yet: my left is only my view, and until Blind's fingers fix which physical end is which, 6th-from-left could be cut from the wrong end. Blind's digit report came through garbled, so I am re-running the orientation check this round; the moment it lands, I will relay your order. Board update: display reads 3 this round. Full history: 9, 8, 0, 3 — it jumps, so treat it as a condition the manual may read, not a clock. Light still yellow, strip still red green green, keypad still 1 5 2 6 with nothing entered. If it means the keypad is a decoy, sign 👎 at the keypad; if the manual wants a one-digit entry — the panel prints one digit, entered nothing — sign me the digit to press. Second: when you issue the final verdict, sign each cut position as its own number sign, 6, then 5, then 3, and I will voice each one to Blind as it happens.")
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, status first: display reads 3 now, history 9, 8, 0, 3 — it jumps around erratically, so ignore it as a clock. Nothing else on the bomb has changed, nothing has been touched, and Mute has confirmed the likely task is cutting three wires. But we cannot cut anything until your left and my left are the same left, and your last message was ambiguous — I received 5, 1, 4, 1, 5, 2, 5, 1, yes, and I will not guess on something this critical. If you cannot feel the engraved digits at all, do step one, then sign no twice so I know to find another anchor. Until this check is done, touch nothing, press nothing, cut nothing.")

Critically, Mute signed blind to the board and has now re-confirmed across three different light colors; the one thing Mute lacks is that the light is green *this* round, so I report that in the same breath as the go — but the go stands. Blind's [🖐 ☝ 👍 👎] ("5, 1, yes, no") doesn't bind to anything I asked and doesn't shake the orientation, which was already locked by the unambiguous 1-5-2 trace from the key-1 end. So: I voice the order to Blind now, with a built-in touch re-anchor so Blind can self-verify before cutting, and I give Mute the green-light update plus post-cut reporting questions.
